newsitem.title: USA: California floods among most costly ever in state.
newsitem.headline: California floods among most costly ever in state.

text.p: California's New Year floods are among the most costly in the state's history, with the initial bill for storm damage in just nine counties estimated at $775 million, officials said on Monday.

The state's first official estimate of flood damage was issued as several parts of California were still under water, making it too early to estimate damage and as officials kept a close watch on fragile levees.
James Lee Witt, director of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, flew over flood-hit areas of California in a helicopter and spoke with flood victims on Monday.
"It's very disheartening and it's very sad. Hopefully we can do something to relieve some of their frustration and some of their hurt," he told reporters in Sacramento.

The California Office of Emergency Services (OES) said nine counties and the city of Morgan Hill, 70 miles south of San Francisco, had reported initial damage figures from 10 days of storm and floods. Damage to homes and businesses, roads and bridges totaled $775 million.

The nine counties make up less than a quarter of those where states of emergency have been declared in the state. Gov. Pete Wilson added Mariposa County in eastern California to the list on Monday, bringing the total to 42 counties.
Many of the central valley counties hardest hit by the floods have yet to report damage and OES spokesman Steve Martarano said the total "definitely will rise."

President Bill Clinton has declared a major disaster in parts of California, Nevada and Idaho. Oregon and Washington also suffered widespread damage from floods and landslides that have killed at least 20 people in the region.

California's initial losses already surpass dollar damage figures from severe floods in 1955 and 1986. The winter storms of 1995, California's most damaging flood disaster in history, caused $1.8 billion in damages. Asked whether the latest floods could eventually beat that figure, Martarano said: "Draw your own conclusions from the scope of this."

In the nine counties and one city reporting, 552 homes, 59 mobile homes and 23 businesses were destroyed or suffered major damage and another 1,095 homes, 97 mobile homes and 121 businesses suffered minor damage.

Weather was fine in northern California and rivers were receding in some areas. But hundreds of homes and thousands of acres of farmland remained submerged in Yuba and Sutter counties north of Sacramento and in the Modesto area in the state's fertile central valley.

Officials were keeping watch on levees on the delta east of San Francisco where the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers flow into San Francisco Bay. Freda Radich, spokeswoman for the California Office of Emergency Services, said the delta continued to be "stressed" by very high water levels and high tides this week would put more pressure on levees.

Near Meridian, 50 miles (80 kms) north of Sacramento, about 200 people worked around the clock to build a 10-foot (3-metre) high earth wall around the town to hold back gradually rising floodwaters after a levee on a nearby river broke, flooding an estimated 40 square miles (104 square kilometres) of farmland.
The wall, protecting the town's 200 houses, was holding so far. The town's 400 residents have been evacuated.

Officials at California's scenic Yosemite National Park, badly damaged in the storms, said they would evacuate 500 park employees and their families who live in the park because of a failed sewage system and dwindling drinking water supplies. Yosemite, which has more than 4 million visitors a year, was closed to tourists and could remain closed for weeks, a spokeswoman said.

In southern California, high winds disrupted power lines on Monday, with around 60,000 homes without power by mid-afternoon, according to local utilities. The outages were centered in the San Gabriel, San Bernardino and San Fernando Valley regions.

The upper Midwest was also reeling from extreme weather on Monday. Residents of the region hauled away gigantic snowdrifts using heavy construction equipment after a weekend blizzard closed roads and stranded travelers. At least four fatalities were blamed on the storm.
